Yes—**you would probably be able to spot the Moon**, despite the bright daylight.

- It is **64° above the horizon**, high in the sky, toward azimuth **120°** (roughly east-southeast).
- At **5.5% illumination**, it is a thin crescent, so it will be much fainter than a half or full Moon.
- Its separation from the Sun is **27°**, which is comfortably wide enough to reduce the risk of it being lost in glare—provided you do **not look near the Sun**.
- A clear sky and normal eyesight are favorable. The main difficulty is that the crescent’s illuminated portion will be small and its unilluminated side will be nearly invisible against the blue sky.

Look about **64° up**, toward the **east-southeast**, and use the Sun’s position only as a reference—never stare at or scan close to it. Binoculars can help you locate the Moon, but use them only after you have safely established the Moon’s position and keep them pointed well away from the Sun.

So: **likely visible to the naked eye, but easy to miss without knowing exactly where to look.**
